title: The three fish
hook: as fishermen come, one fish leaves early, one plays dead, one is caught (Masnavi 4.2202ff)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bitter cucumber: throw it away, step around the briars. Step aside.

The check engine light comes on, and you tell yourself you'll deal with it next week. The tooth that twinges when you drink something cold. The friend who's been quiet for a month. The small voice at work that says this project is heading for the rocks. A lot of trouble sends a warning first. The question is what we do in the gap between the warning and the net. Rumi tells an old story, from a book of animal fables older than he was, about three fish in a lake, and the day the fishermen came by.
screen: `THE CHECK ENGINE LIGHT.` → `BETWEEN THE WARNING AND THE NET.` → `THE THREE FISH.`

segments.voice: It's in Book Four of the Masnavi. In a lake lived three fish: one wise, one half-wise, and one foolish. One day some fishermen walk past, notice the fish, and hurry off to get their net. The wise fish decides right then: I'm leaving. The lake connects to the sea; the way is hard, but it goes at once. And Rumi adds a detail. It doesn't stop to consult the others, because they'd talk it out of going. Home is comfortable, and comfort is persuasive. So it makes the long trip alone and reaches the open sea. The half-wise fish waits. When the fishermen come back with the net, it's too late to leave, and it's sorry it didn't go with its friend. But it has one good idea. It plays dead, floating belly up. The fisherman picks it up, thinks, a dead fish, and tosses it aside, and it slips quietly back into the water and gets away. The foolish fish does neither. It thrashes in panic, jumping this way and that, and the net closes on it. It ends in the frying pan. Rumi himself points readers to Kalila and Dimna for the tale, and a version also appears in the Indian Panchatantra. He reads it his own way. The wise fish is the soul that acts on the first sign, before the net arrives. The half-wise one survives by a kind of dying, like the parrot a few weeks ago. The foolish one waits and flails. Your line: leave in time.
screen: `ONE WISE, ONE HALF-WISE, ONE FOOLISH.` · `THE WISE FISH GOES AT ONCE, ALONE.` · `THE HALF-WISE FISH PLAYS DEAD.` · then, large: `LEAVE IN TIME.`

segments.voice: Let one small warning in your life come to mind, a sound in the car, a bill, a strained friendship, a habit getting stronger, and notice how you've been waiting. Picture the smallest first move you could make: a phone call, an appointment, one honest sentence. Don't consult the part of you that loves the lake.
Fish. When fishermen come, one fish leaves at once, one plays dead and escapes, and one flails and is caught. Today's word.
Your line: leave in time. The wise fish didn't wait for the net. Day two hundred ten.

howItsDone: The fable appears in the Panchatantra, in Kalila and Dimna and in Rumi; some Sufi readers take it as a call to respond to the first stirrings of conscience.

fork.setup: you're a fish in a lake. fishermen have just walked by and gone to fetch a net. what does the wise fish do?
options: ask the others what they think.
leave for the sea at once, alone.
wait and see if they really come back.
fork.reveal: it left immediately, without consulting anyone, and reached the open sea.

original.note: Persian: a fish. Rumi's three fish are the wise, the half-wise and the foolish.
